recent_posts.title: Why you should tell your manager what you want for your career
recent_posts.summary: Staying silent about career goals in 1:1s is a common but costly habit. When you explicitly tell your manager what you want — a promotion, a lead role, a team change — they can actually help you get there. Managers work with incomplete information and can't advocate for you if they don't know your direction. Saying your goal out loud also makes it real, shifting you from passive daydreaming to active pursuit. The risk of speaking up is far smaller than years of quiet resentment over opportunities you never asked for.

recent_posts.title: “Good Taste” Is Just Experience
recent_posts.summary: The popular claim that 'taste is the ultimate differentiator in the AI era' is misleading because it frames a learnable skill as an innate gift. What people call taste is actually pattern recognition built through years of experience and repetition. This framing is harmful to junior developers who hear it and assume they're permanently behind. The real message should be 'you need reps' — show up, review code, ship features, and the intuition will develop over time.

recent_posts.title: How engineering incentives reward complexity and punish simplicity
recent_posts.summary: Engineering teams systematically reward over-engineering while penalizing simplicity, creating perverse incentives from interviews to promotions. Engineers who build elaborate systems get compelling narratives for promotion packets, while those who ship clean, minimal solutions have nothing impressive to show. The post argues that unearned complexity is the real problem, not complexity itself, and offers concrete advice: engineers should document the decisions they didn't make and frame their judgment explicitly, while engineering leaders should change the questions asked in design reviews and promotion discussions to make simplicity the default rather than something that needs defending.

recent_posts.title: State your position before asking for opinions
recent_posts.summary: Asking "what do you think?" without stating your own position first offloads cognitive work onto others and slows down decision-making. Instead of vague questions, share your recommendation with reasoning, alternatives considered, and an assumed path forward. This transforms collaboration from "help me think" into "check my thinking," reducing ambiguity and enabling faster decisions. Even when uncertain, stating a position gives teammates something concrete to react to rather than forcing them to do all the analytical work themselves.

recent_posts.title: Why I Still Write Code as an Engineering Manager
recent_posts.summary: An engineering manager explains why they continue writing code despite management responsibilities. They focus on non-critical work like bug fixes and tooling improvements to stay connected to the codebase, demonstrate quality standards through their own PRs and code reviews, and maintain credibility with their team. By experiencing the same developer pain points firsthand, they can make better decisions about technical debt, deadlines, and process improvements while showing rather than telling what good work looks like.

recent_posts.title: Why consuming content at 1x speed improves retention and intentionality
recent_posts.summary: Consuming content at 2x speed has become a productivity badge, but it often stems from FOMO and anxiety rather than genuine efficiency. Slowing down to 1x speed forces intentional content selection: if something isn't worth full attention, it's not worth consuming at all. This approach reduces throughput but increases retention, enjoyment, and creates mental space for original thinking. The constant optimization for consuming more content leaves no room for boredom, which is where ideas emerge and learning gets processed. Switching to 1x acts as a quality filter, making you ruthless about what deserves your time.

recent_posts.title: How a software engineering blog reached 230,000 readers by focusing on soft skills
recent_posts.summary: A software engineering blog reached 230,000 unique visitors in its first year by focusing on the human side of engineering rather than technical frameworks. The most popular posts covered topics like what makes engineers senior, workplace politics, management repair skills, and how strengths can become weaknesses. The success came from addressing a gap in content about soft skills, interpersonal dynamics, and career navigation that technical professionals struggle with but rarely discuss.

recent_posts.title: Engineers dismissing AI coding tools based on outdated experiences are falling behind
recent_posts.summary: Many engineers dismiss AI coding tools based on outdated experiences from 2022-2023, without trying modern versions like Claude Code or Cursor. These tools have improved dramatically, enabling engineers to ship faster and tackle bigger challenges. While AI-generated code still requires review and isn't perfect, refusing to try current tools creates a widening gap between engineers who leverage them and those who don't. Engineers should test modern AI coding assistants to make informed judgments rather than relying on years-old impressions.

recent_posts.title: “ChatGPT said this” Is Lazy
recent_posts.summary: Pasting AI-generated responses in code reviews without context or personal understanding is lazy and counterproductive. While AI tools like ChatGPT can help explore ideas, reviewers must provide specific, contextual feedback in their own words. Good reviews require real engagement with the code, understanding of business constraints, and accountability—things AI cannot provide. Use AI to help you think, not to avoid thinking.

recent_posts.title: Give feedback only when there is measurable impact
recent_posts.summary: Most manager feedback stems from personal preference rather than measurable impact. Before giving feedback, verify it addresses concrete issues: measurable work outcomes, team collaboration problems, or hostile environment creation. Feedback without demonstrable impact creates fatigue, reduces psychological safety, and pressures conformity over diversity. When behavior bothers you but doesn't affect results, manage your own discomfort instead of policing personality differences. Effective feedback focuses on helping people contribute toward shared goals, not creating uniform behavior patterns.
